The problem with AI is that, this time, nobody was caught off guard. From small startups to tech giants, everyone bet heavily on it. There are very good open-weight Chinese models, and even a French miracle. There is no winner-take-all.

So models are already a commodity, and will remain one for years. Companies must balance capex with very long payback periods against strict austerity everywhere else.

Good news for customers, BTW.

I think a lot of companies are struggling to move beyond this being a thing developers use to something everyone can use. Developers have to go really far out of their way to build agents and tools that apply the capabilities to their specific business. Someone in accounting cannot simply fire up chatgpt.com or copilot and use it in the same way a developer can. There is no instruction manual or historical precedent for how to do this. Very few people are currently in the right situation to make this work.

My observation is that most development teams are still in panic / survival mode, spending all day stacking sandbags instead of bringing these capabilities to the broader team. The fear of job loss in this particular market is crippling. No one will admit it publicly but you can feel the adversity on every AI status call. I've managed to convince a few that AI won't take their jobs, and these people have become indispensable at enabling deployment of AI beyond the weird nerd part of the org chart.

How does this affect OpenAI's prospects in the next few quarters?

Unlike Anthropic, OAI does not have an S-1 to pore over. Their finances are shrouded in rumor and speculation. I can't assess how much of a death knell a ~15B financing shortfall is.

Look. Some say AI improves speed. It might also improve quality - if you use it as a tool, with a full understanding of what's happening in your system and preserved ability to maintain that system even if AI disappears one day for whatever reason. But since all the competitors are jumping into AI, most won't focus on quality, but on delivering speed, as you have to be competitive and justify AI cost, right? So if AI doesn't improve relative speed, and in many cases doesn't improve quality, then why is it there? The possible answer is: to consolidate the means of production under one's own control. With AI and robots involvement, humanity might be forced into an anti-utopia.
